title: Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm

concept.text: The innovation is an actual quantum execution of Shor’s algorithm that solves a cryptographic instance at a deployed key size: for example, factoring a 2048-bit RSA modulus or recovering a discrete logarithm for a public key on a deployed 256-bit elliptic curve. Shor’s algorithm already supplies the mathematical method. The missing advance is a quantum computer capable of completing the required computation reliably, with independently checkable answers and evidence that the quantum device produced them.

This is an execution milestone. A resource estimate describes a possible machine; a small compiled experiment demonstrates selected algorithmic operations; a cryptographically relevant execution must carry the computation through at the target scale. The supplied studies describe routes toward that capability and useful component demonstrations, but do not demonstrate its achievement.

significance.text: Successful execution would turn a theoretical quantum threat into an experimentally demonstrated ability to recover secrets underlying widely deployed public-key cryptography. For an RSA instance the machine can factor, the factors undermine the corresponding RSA security. For an elliptic-curve public key whose discrete logarithm it can recover, the result exposes the associated private key. The revolutionary consequence is a concrete break of security resting on those mathematical problems and parameters.

The consequences would depend on the protocol and the information available to an attacker. Recorded traffic could become decryptable where captured protocol data and recovered secrets suffice; this does not imply that every recorded internet session becomes readable. Cryptocurrency exposure would likewise depend on the scheme and public-key exposure. The cat-qubit compilation paper identifies exposed public keys, including certain Bitcoin outputs and reused addresses, as relevant attack targets rather than establishing a threat to every asset.

One successful RSA factorization would not itself demonstrate an elliptic-curve attack, and success on one curve would not establish practical attacks on every deployed curve. Additional targets require suitable circuits, resources and runtimes. A universal machine’s existence alone is insufficient: its usable scale and reliability must support the relevant computation. Migration to quantum-resistant cryptography is a response to this threat, while the milestone itself is the verified factorization or discrete logarithm accompanied by evidence of quantum execution.

Conceptual synthesis: an expensive, slow or specialized implementation could still establish this breakthrough. Its operating cost and throughput would determine how broadly the capability could be used. Success would neither automatically deliver other quantum applications nor prove that factoring is classically hard; those are separate scientific questions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is sustained, fault-tolerant execution of a cryptographically sized factoring or discrete-logarithm circuit. This requires enough protected computational capacity, sufficiently reliable operations, and coordinated error correction and classical control to complete the entire calculation. Qubit count alone does not establish feasibility: the estimates also depend on connectivity, error models, correction-cycle speed and the time needed to react to measurement outcomes.

For the surface-code route, the engineering challenge includes realizing the assumed square nearest-neighbor architecture with uniform 0.1% depolarizing gate noise, 1 μs correction cycles and 10 μs reaction time at the required scale. Gidney’s estimate also contains algorithmic and architectural assumptions, and leaves further analysis of cold storage to future work. These assumptions define a conditional route to the target, rather than a complete experimental validation of every subsystem.

For the cat-qubit route, suppressing one error channel does not eliminate the need to control the other. The most compact supplied estimate assumes negligible bit flips, interpreted as a bit-flip time of about 100 years, while also assuming a phase-flip probability of 5 × 10⁻⁴ per 1 μs correction cycle. Allowing a bit-flip time of about one hour requires an additional protection layer and roughly doubles the estimated qubit count. A controlled single cat qubit with long bit-flip lifetime does not establish that thousands of interacting qubits can maintain the full set of assumed properties throughout a multiday computation.

Engineering synthesis: the central integration barrier is preserving the required performance while combining qubits, gates, measurements, error correction and classical processing into one operating machine. Comparing architectures therefore requires their complete noise and timing assumptions, rather than comparing headline qubit counts or isolated memory lifetimes.

current_state.text: Enrique Martín-López and collaborators’ 2012 Nature Photonics experiment demonstrated a compiled two-photon implementation that factored N = 21 using qubit recycling. Its circuit was constructed for the particular case N = 21 and x = 4, using known structure and explicitly calculated evolution. It demonstrated meaningful quantum interference and scalable recycling ideas, but was not a cryptographic-scale factorization. This historical result does not establish the worldwide experimental frontier in 2026.

Craig Gidney’s arXiv work submitted on 21 May 2025 estimates that a 2048-bit RSA integer could be factored in less than a week using fewer than one million noisy qubits. The stated physical assumptions include a square nearest-neighbor grid, uniform 0.1% depolarizing gate noise, a 1 μs surface-code cycle and a 10 μs reaction time. This is a conditional resource estimate, not a hardware execution. The supplied review had the complete 40-page paper available; it also identified additional algorithmic assumptions and deferred cold-storage analysis.

The cat-qubit compilation preprint by Axel Pappalardo, Dahmun Goudarzi and collaborators, dated 27 October 2026, estimates RSA-2048 factoring with 22,593 cat qubits—approximately 23,000—in 3.14 days. That configuration assumes 1 μs error-correction cycles, 10 μs reaction time, phase-flip probability pZ = 5 × 10⁻⁴ and negligible bit flips, corresponding to a bit-flip time of about 100 years. With a bit-flip time of about one hour, an additional protection layer raises the estimate to approximately 45,000 cat qubits and a runtime of at least 3.14 days. These figures describe projected configurations under different error assumptions.

The retained extraction of that 128-page cat-qubit paper ends on page 30. Its visible sections support the quoted estimates and benchmark discussion, but the detailed derivation in Appendix C9 and the experimental-state appendix were outside the available extraction. Consequently, the supplied material permits reporting those estimates but does not support treating the entire derivation or its survey of hardware progress as fully examined.

U. Réglade and collaborators’ 2024 Nature paper reports control of a single cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds. The associated author responses report phase-flip times ranging from 2.7 μs at cat size |α|² = 2.5 to 490 ns at |α|² = 11.3. These are measurements at different cat sizes, so they should not be combined into one simultaneous operating point. They also rule out the blanket characterization that phase-flip times were all below one microsecond. The main article was available as a subscription preview; the phase-flip range comes from the associated peer-review file.

The reported single-qubit experiment does not demonstrate the hour-scale or century-scale bit-flip times assumed in the two cited factoring configurations, nor does it demonstrate a complete factoring machine. The supplied evidence contains no cryptographically relevant execution. It also contains no comprehensive freshness survey establishing worldwide nonachievement as of 1 November 2026. The retained arXiv versions establish preprint provenance, but do not establish the absence of later journal publication. Those limits leave current global status open; they do not invalidate the dated experiments or resource estimates.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: execute quantum factoring of an independently selected standard 2048-bit RSA modulus whose factors are initially unknown to the demonstrators, or recover the discrete logarithm of an independently selected public key on a deployed 256-bit elliptic curve whose private key is initially unknown to them. These are proposed milestones grounded in the supplied cryptographic benchmarks, not established consensus standards. Either would establish the corresponding capability at that target size.
completion_criteria.label: Quantum-solve unknown 2048-bit RSA or unknown 256-bit elliptic discrete log

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: publish the factors or recovered discrete logarithm, the circuit and compilation method, device description, runtime, measurement records and classical processing needed to assess the execution. Multiplication can verify a factorization, and the corresponding public-key calculation can verify a recovered discrete logarithm. Correctness of the answer and evidence of its quantum provenance are separate requirements; a correct answer alone does not establish that a quantum device computed it.
completion_criteria.label: Published verifiable factors or discrete log with quantum provenance records

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: repeat the demonstration on additional independently selected instances and make the procedure sufficiently explicit for independent assessment and, where feasible, replication. Report success rates, failed attempts, total runtime, physical resources and classical processing costs. Such finite tests establish demonstrated breadth and operating reliability; they do not establish literal universality across all moduli, curves or implementations. Commercially attractive cost or throughput would be a further practical achievement, rather than a prerequisite for the first convincing execution.
completion_criteria.label: Assessable repeats on independent instances with reliability and resource costs

completion_criteria.text: A compiled circuit for a preselected tiny integer would not satisfy this proposal. The N = 21 experiment illustrates why: a circuit built around a known small instance can demonstrate valuable quantum operations without establishing the ability to solve an independently chosen cryptographic problem. The relevant distinction is the demonstrated computational scope and treatment of prior knowledge.
completion_criteria.label: Independently chosen cryptographic problem solved without prior knowledge

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation,” concerns a general ability to preserve and process quantum information as protection increases. QUA-02 concerns completing one demanding cryptographic application. General fault-tolerant capability is closely relevant to its implementation, but demonstrating that capability alone does not establish completion of the required cryptographic circuit.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04, “A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature,” and QUA-05, “Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons,” concern distinct physical approaches to quantum protection or computation. Either could be relevant to a future implementation, but passive storage or braiding-based universality would not itself demonstrate cryptographic execution. QUA-06, “Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules,” addresses a possible scaling mechanism rather than the cryptographic result.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-08, “Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls,” addresses the cost of obtaining reliable computation. QUA-02 could be achieved with high overhead, while lower overhead could make later executions more practical. The supplied title supports this distinction, but does not establish QUA-08’s detailed technical requirements or whether it would precede or follow QUA-02. QUA-10, “Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator,” similarly specifies a manufacturing and operating platform that QUA-02 does not require.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-07, “A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems,” is a complexity-theoretic separation. Executing Shor’s algorithm at a deployed key size would not prove that separation or prove classical factoring hardness. Conversely, a complexity separation would not by itself supply a working cryptographic attack.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” and QUA-09, “An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data,” concern different application outcomes and evidence requirements. They overlap with QUA-02 in requiring more than an abstract algorithm or isolated component demonstration, but a successful cryptographic execution would not establish either material prediction or an end-to-end speedup on large classical data.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the worldwide frontier of Shor experiments or hardware as of 1 November 2026, including whether a cryptographically relevant execution has occurred elsewhere.
Whether either retained arXiv work has a later journal publication is not established.
The detailed cat-qubit derivation in Appendix C9 and its experimental-state appendix were outside the retained extraction.
The extent to which either projected architecture can sustain all assumed noise, connectivity and timing properties simultaneously at full scale remains unestablished by the supplied experiments.
Detailed technical relationships and relative timing among the roster concepts, particularly QUA-08, cannot be determined from titles alone.

brief.title: Quantum computers that break widely used encryption
possible: Secrets protected by RSA, an encryption system, could be recovered by a quantum computer that splits its large public number into its hidden factors. The target is an actual calculation on a 2048-bit number using Shor’s algorithm, the mathematical method for doing this.

Another target is recovering the private key behind a public key on a deployed 256-bit elliptic curve, a mathematical structure used in cryptography. Either achievement would need a checkable answer and evidence that the quantum computer produced it.
why: For people and organisations relying on these systems, this would turn a mathematical threat into a demonstrated security break. Recovering the hidden factors or private key would undermine the protection of the corresponding key.
Some recorded communications could become readable when the recovered secrets and recorded data suffice. Cryptocurrency holdings protected by exposed public keys could also face attacks.

sources.showed: Gidney estimated the hardware needed for quantum factoring of RSA numbers. His design reduced quantum memory requirements and the count of Toffoli gates, a type of quantum logic operation.
sources.cited_for: The calculation gives a conditional route to breaking RSA with fewer qubits, the basic units of quantum computing.
sources.not_established: A hardware estimate does not demonstrate a machine completing the calculation.

sources.who: Enrique Martín-López and collaborators, University of Bristol
sources.showed: The team factored 21 with a quantum circuit tailored to that small problem. They reused a control qubit rather than providing a separate one for each stage.
sources.quote:
The algorithmic output is distinguishable from noise, in contrast to
previous demonstrations.
sources.cited_for: The experiment demonstrated useful quantum operations and a way to reduce memory requirements.
sources.not_established: A circuit tailored to a known small problem does not establish cryptographic-scale factoring.

sources.who: Axel Pappalardo, Dahmun Goudarzi and collaborators
sources.showed: The preprint mapped factoring onto proposed chip layouts using cat qubits, quantum bits designed to resist accidental switches between stored values. It estimated hardware and runtime under assumed error rates.
sources.quote:
Together, these
compilations lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048.
sources.cited_for: Cat qubits offer another proposed route to a complete cryptographic attack.
sources.not_established: The proposed machine has not demonstrated the required error protection and control throughout a full calculation.

sources.showed: The team controlled a cat qubit while preserving its protection against bit flips, accidental switches between stored values.
sources.quote: we implemented a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding 10 s.
sources.cited_for: The experiment showed that quantum control can preserve a cat qubit’s built-in protection.
sources.not_established: This component demonstration falls short of the protection lifetimes and interacting hardware required by the factoring estimates.

shown: Martín-López and colleagues demonstrated factoring a small number with a specially tailored circuit. Réglade and colleagues demonstrated protected control of a cat qubit. These are component demonstrations, rather than complete attacks on deployed encryption.

Gidney estimated a factoring machine using fewer than a million noisy qubits. Pappalardo, Goudarzi and colleagues proposed a different machine using cat qubits. Both calculations depend on hardware meeting demanding error and timing assumptions.
missing: A complete quantum calculation must solve an independently chosen cryptographic problem whose answer was initially unknown to the team.
Enough interacting qubits must maintain reliable operations, error correction and classical control throughout the calculation.
Public results and execution details must establish both a correct answer and its quantum origin.
Repeated runs on independent problems must establish success rates and total resource costs.

milestones.label: An unknown cryptographic problem solved at the target size
milestones.explanation: A quantum computer would have to factor an independently chosen RSA number or recover an elliptic-curve private key at the specified key size, with the answer initially unknown. Either would establish the corresponding attack.

milestones.label: A checkable answer with evidence of quantum execution
milestones.explanation: The team would have to publish the answer, circuit, device details, runtime, measurements and classical processing. This would let others assess correctness and whether the quantum device produced the answer.

milestones.label: Repeated successes with measured reliability and costs
milestones.explanation: Further independently chosen problems would have to be solved with assessable procedures and reported failures, success rates and costs. This would establish demonstrated breadth and operating reliability.

milestones.label: An independent problem solved without prior knowledge
milestones.explanation: The demonstration would have to solve an independently chosen cryptographic problem without knowing its answer beforehand. This would distinguish the capability from a circuit tailored around a known tiny example.

uncertain: Can either proposed machine sustain all its assumed error rates, connections and control speeds throughout a full calculation?
How much repetition would establish convincing reliability across independently chosen problems?
Success on one cryptographic target would leave the resources and runtime needed for other targets open.

page.title: Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm
page.definition: A quantum processor runs the period-finding part of Shor’s algorithm. Classical processing of its measurements yields either the two primes whose product is the 2048-bit RSA challenge number or the secret scalar of a public point on secp256k1, a 256-bit elliptic curve used in Bitcoin. The scalar is the discrete logarithm: it tells how many copies of the public base point add up to the supplied point.

goal.need: The estimated cost to migrate priority U.S. federal systems to post-quantum cryptography or replace incompatible systems is $7.1 billion. Operators assessing threats to confidential traffic and digital signatures rely on estimates of future hardware. A run at a deployed key size would give them a measured qubit count and time for the affected key type. For traffic that must remain confidential for years, protection requires changing vulnerable key exchange before anyone records the traffic.

completion.title: Quantum Shor execution factors RSA-2048 or recovers a secp256k1 private scalar.
completion.criterion: Execute Shor’s algorithm on quantum hardware to factor RSA Laboratories’ RSA-2048 challenge number, or recover an initially unknown scalar k from Q = kG on secp256k1, whose base point G has 256-bit order. The solution must come from the quantum computation and satisfy pq = N for prime factors p and q, or kG = Q for the recovered scalar. Each branch establishes only its corresponding cryptographic capability.
completion.set_by: Alice & Bob and collaborators, Pappalardo et al., Sections I–II: proposed cryptanalytic benchmarking protocol in a preprint, not a certification standard.
completion.threshold_quote: Shor’s algorithm applied respectively to RSA-2048 challenge number, Bitcoin curve (secp256k1)
completion.basis: Pappalardo and colleagues specify the problem instances and compare qubit count and execution time without setting a time or repetition cutoff. RFC 9958 defines cryptographic relevance in terms of a practical attack time. The 2022 Quantum Threat Timeline Report asks specifically about factoring a 2048-bit number in less than 24 hours. Gidney’s estimate of under a week with fewer than one million noisy qubits assumes square-grid nearest-neighbor connectivity, 0.1% gate error, 1 μs correction cycles and 10 μs control response. GAO reported in October 2026 that current hardware could not break deployed public-key cryptography.

milestones.title: A small factoring circuit produces an order-finding signal distinguishable from noise.
milestones.criterion: Run the quantum order-finding circuit for a small factoring instance. Show that the measured output distribution exhibits the expected period information and can be distinguished from the distribution produced by noise.
milestones.set_by: Martín-López et al., experimental quantum order-finding protocol for factoring.
milestones.threshold_quote: The algorithmic output is distinguishable from noise, in contrast to previous demonstrations.

milestones.title: Quantum error correction creates a logical qubit with lower error than its physical constituents.
milestones.criterion: Encode at least one logical qubit and run quantum error correction. Compare the encoded and physical implementations of the same task under comparable conditions and demonstrate a lower error rate for the logical qubit.
milestones.set_by: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Quantum Computing: Progress and Prospects, Section 7.3.4, milestone G2b.
milestones.threshold_quote: one or more logical qubits of better error rates than possible with physical qubits

milestones.title: Encoded qubits implement a universal fault-tolerant gate set.
milestones.criterion: Implement a fault-tolerant set of operations on encoded qubits sufficient to approximate arbitrary quantum circuits. One qualifying set consists of the single-qubit Hadamard and T gates together with an entangling controlled-NOT gate.
milestones.set_by: German Federal Office for Information Security, Status of quantum computer development, section 3.3.4, elementary fault-tolerant gates.
milestones.threshold_quote: The requirement is the ability to carry out a universal gate set.

milestones.title: A quantum processor recovers an 80-bit discrete logarithm modulo a 512-bit prime.
milestones.criterion: For the FFDLP-512 benchmark, run Shor’s algorithm on quantum hardware to recover the initially unknown 80-bit exponent x from h = g^x mod p, where p is a 512-bit prime. Verify that the recovered exponent satisfies the equation.
milestones.set_by: Alice & Bob and collaborators, Pappalardo et al., Section I and Appendix D.2. This proposed intermediate benchmark specifically reuses the RSA implementation.
milestones.threshold_quote: a 512-bit prime group and an 80-bit exponent.

milestones.title: A quantum processor runs the N = 15 instance of Shor’s factoring algorithm.
milestones.criterion: Execute the order-finding circuit for N = 15 on quantum hardware and obtain measurements from which the prime factors can be recovered by classical processing.
milestones.set_by: Vandersypen et al., N = 15 experimental factoring protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: the simplest instance of Shor's algorithm: factorization of N = 15

milestones.title: A documented Shor run on quantum hardware recovers a small elliptic-curve private key.
milestones.criterion: Recover an elliptic-curve private scalar from its public key using Shor’s algorithm on a quantum computer. Supply the hardware description, code, circuit details, full logs and validation data. The prize rules rank qualifying entries by key length and specify no minimum bit length.
milestones.set_by: Project Eleven, The QDay Prize Competition Official Rules, sections 5.2–5.3 and 8.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: Run Shor’s Algorithm on a quantum computer to crack the largest elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) you can.

milestones.title: A quantum memory’s logical error per correction cycle falls as code distance increases.
milestones.criterion: Operate quantum memories from the same error-correcting code family at increasing code distances under comparable physical conditions. Measure the logical error per correction cycle at each distance and demonstrate suppression with increasing distance.
milestones.set_by: Below-threshold quantum memory scaling, as tested by Acharya et al. and identified in section 8.5.1 of the German Federal Office for Information Security’s evaluation scheme.
milestones.threshold_quote: the logical error rate is suppressed exponentially as more qubits are added

not_found: No published hardware execution satisfying the RSA-2048, secp256k1 or FFDLP-512 benchmark was located.
No regulator or standards-body acceptance protocol for quantum provenance in a cryptographic-scale Shor execution was located.
Independent confirmation that the 15-bit QDay Prize run produced a quantum signal distinguishable from noise was not located.

definition = "A quantum processor runs the period-finding part of Shor\u2019s algorithm. Classical processing of its measurements yields either the two primes whose product is the 2048-bit RSA challenge number or the secret scalar of a public point on secp256k1, a 256-bit elliptic curve used in Bitcoin. The scalar is the discrete logarithm: it tells how many copies of the public base point add up to the supplied point.". Reason: The definition now identifies which part must run on quantum hardware and explains both mathematical outputs.

goal.need = "The estimated cost to migrate priority U.S. federal systems to post-quantum cryptography or replace incompatible systems is $7.1 billion. Operators assessing threats to confidential traffic and digital signatures rely on estimates of future hardware. A run at a deployed key size would give them a measured qubit count and time for the affected key type. For traffic that must remain confidential for years, protection requires changing vulnerable key exchange before anyone records the traffic.". Reason: The existing paragraph omits the scale of migration, the decision a measured result would inform and the reason confidentiality cannot wait for a demonstration.

add statement by National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019: "run Shor’s algorithm to break RSA 2048". Reason: The National Academies’ milestone summary explicitly identifies the RSA capability.

edit completion: basis = "Pappalardo and colleagues specify the problem instances and compare qubit count and execution time without setting a time or repetition cutoff. RFC 9958 defines cryptographic relevance in terms of a practical attack time. The 2022 Quantum Threat Timeline Report asks specifically about factoring a 2048-bit number in less than 24 hours. Gidney\u2019s estimate of under a week with fewer than one million noisy qubits assumes square-grid nearest-neighbor connectivity, 0.1% gate error, 1 \u03bcs correction cycles and 10 \u03bcs control response. GAO reported in October 2026 that current hardware could not break deployed public-key cryptography."; refs = [4, 5, 6, 7, 3, 29]. Reason: The basis now distinguishes an untimed instance benchmark from the practical-time definition used in security guidance and the explicit time limit used in threat surveys.

add milestone after None: "A quantum processor runs the N = 15 instance of Shor’s factoring algorithm.". Reason: The first laboratory factoring experiment preceded the stronger signal-versus-noise test by eleven years.

edit m1: title = "A small factoring circuit produces an order-finding signal distinguishable from noise."; criterion = "Run the quantum order-finding circuit for a small factoring instance. Show that the measured output distribution exhibits the expected period information and can be distinguished from the distribution produced by noise."; set_by = "Mart\u00edn-L\u00f3pez et al., experimental quantum order-finding protocol for factoring."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "The algorithmic output is distinguishable from noise, in contrast to previous demonstrations."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 16]. Reason: The cited protocol tests factoring, and its measured result belongs outside the criterion.

add milestone after m1: "A documented Shor run on quantum hardware recovers a small elliptic-curve private key.". Reason: The QDay Prize supplies a hardware and documentation test for the elliptic-curve branch where the entry had extrapolated from a factoring experiment.

edit m2: criterion = "Encode at least one logical qubit and run quantum error correction. Compare the encoded and physical implementations of the same task under comparable conditions and demonstrate a lower error rate for the logical qubit."; threshold_quote = "one or more logical qubits of better error rates than possible with physical qubits"; threshold_ref = 9. Reason: The criterion mixed the logical-qubit comparison with results for two experiments that measured different kinds of protection.

add milestone after m2: "A quantum memory’s logical error per correction cycle falls as code distance increases.". Reason: A comparison at one code size leaves open whether adding physical qubits further suppresses logical errors.

edit m3: criterion = "Implement a fault-tolerant set of operations on encoded qubits sufficient to approximate arbitrary quantum circuits. One qualifying set consists of the single-qubit Hadamard and T gates together with an entangling controlled-NOT gate."; set_by = "German Federal Office for Information Security, Status of quantum computer development, section 3.3.4, elementary fault-tolerant gates."; set_by_kind = "government_programme"; threshold_quote = "The requirement is the ability to carry out a universal gate set."; threshold_ref = 28; refs = [28, 12, 20, 24]. Reason: The federal evaluation scheme states the universal-gate requirement directly, and the revised criterion removes a particular device’s results.
